newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina police and jobless clash again in Jujuy.
newsitem.headline: Argentina police and jobless clash again in Jujuy.

text.p: Argentine military police and hundreds of unemployed sugar workers clashed for the second consecutive day on Thursday in the poor northwestern province of Jujuy, with at least 80 people injured.

The paramilitary police used tear gas, rubber bullets and truncheons against a crowd of about 500 laid-off sugar workers and their families who have been blocking National Highway 34 to demand new jobs and state aid.
Sixty people, among them three policemen, were hurt in clashes on Wednesday along the highway where the protesters burned tires and set up makeshift soup kitchens.

Heavy-handed police action in Jujuy, and in separate incidents involving street-hawkers and students in the city of La Plata near Buenos Aires on Wednesday, earned reprimands from the Catholic church and trade union leaders.

But Peronist President Carlos Menem, who blames the unrest on "presubversive gymnastics" encouraged by the opposition, issued a statement saying the riots were provoked by agitators who "prefer the sterile path of violence and put infiltrators among citizens of good faith."
"Unemployment cannot be turned into a matter for agitators and social unrest," said Menem. "This government has the duty to maintain order."
The main CGT labour federation declared itself "on permanent alert to fight repression and unemployment."
The unions blame Menem's free-market reforms for a jobless rate which has risen to more than 17 percent from six percent when he came to power in 1989, and for rising poverty indicators.

Roadblock protests against unemployment and poverty have cropped up as far apart as Patagonia in the south -- where a bystander was recently shot and killed, apparently by military police -- and the northwest desert provinces of Salta and Jujuy.
The dearth of jobs has forced people to seek a precarious living from street stalls, which the hawkers of La Plata were defending against inspectors when Wednesday's riots began.
"The needs imposed by current economic model cannot be assuaged with tear gas, truncheons and bullets, or silenced with false promises," said the CGT in a statement.

The head of the Argentine Catholic Church's social affairs wing, Monsignor Rafael Rey, accused the government of "trying to repress instead of hold a dialogue. You cannot just crack down like that on people who want to work and earn a living."
Menem's government, warned by the International Monetary Fund's Michel Camdessus on Wednesday of the risks of neglecting the poor, announced a $600 million boost to social welfare.
